job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

passage: Teacher: Today, let us discuss probability. Imagine we toss a coin 10 times and get 8 heads. What is the experimental probability of getting a head? Rahul: Is it 8 divided by 2, because we have two outcomes? Teacher: Not quite, Rahul. Experimental probability is the number of successful trials divided by the total number of trials. So, it is 8/10. Priya: But teacher, if we toss it 1000 times, the result will be exactly 500 heads, right? Teacher: Not necessarily. As the number of trials increases, the experimental probability gets closer to the theoretical probability, but they are rarely identical. Rahul: What if the probability of an event is 0.4? Does that mean the probability of it not happening is also 0.4? Teacher: No, the sum of the probabilities of an event and its complement is always 1. So, if P(E) is 0.4, P(not E) must be 0.6. Priya: I once read that a probability can be 5/4 if the event is very likely. Teacher: That is incorrect. A probability value must always lie between 0 and 1 inclusive. It can never exceed 1, as the number of favourable outcomes cannot exceed the total possible outcomes.

items.evidence: Experimental probability is the number of successful trials divided by the total number of trials.
items.q: A coin is tossed 20 times and shows heads 12 times. What is the experimental probability of a head?
items.explain: Experimental probability is successful trials divided by total trials, so 12 out of 20.

wrong.why: repeats Rahul's mistake of dividing by the two outcomes
thinks two outcomes always means 1/2 each

items.evidence: As the number of trials increases, the experimental probability gets closer to the theoretical probability, but they are rarely identical.
items.q: Priya tosses a fair coin 1000 times. What will her experimental probability of heads most likely be?
options: Still 8/10, the same as ten tosses
No closer to 1/2 than ten tosses
items.explain: With more trials, experimental probability gets closer to theoretical probability, but they are rarely identical.

wrong.why: thinks experimental must exactly equal theoretical
treats one small test as a fixed rule
thinks 10 trials are as reliable as 1000

items.evidence: No, the sum of the probabilities of an event and its complement is always 1.
items.q: The probability of rain tomorrow is 0.7. What is the probability that it will not rain?
items.explain: An event and its complement add up to 1, so 1 − 0.7 = 0.3.

wrong.why: repeats Rahul's idea that the complement has the same value
adds instead of subtracting, accepting a probability above 1
thinks 0.7 means it will definitely rain

items.evidence: It can never exceed 1, as the number of favourable outcomes cannot exceed the total possible outcomes.
items.q: Meena works out that an event has probability 5/4. What should she conclude?
options: Her answer is wrong, as it is above 1
Her event is extremely likely to happen
Her event will happen more than once
Her answer is right if outcomes are unequal
items.explain: Probability lies between 0 and 1, since favourable outcomes cannot exceed total outcomes.

wrong.why: believes, like Priya, that likely events can exceed 1
reads a value above 1 as happening repeatedly
thinks the 0 to 1 rule depends on the outcomes
